entry.summary: Frontend testing used to sound simple: open a page, find an element, click it, and verify the result. That description still works for basic workflows, but modern interfaces are no longer a single static DOM that changes in obvious ways. Components can render inside Shadow DOM. entry.title: In Kiro We Trust
entry.summary: Two years ago, a surgeon friend pitched me a SaaS idea he wanted us to build together. He had zero development background and assumed I could just make it happen, but the reality of building a full application (backend, frontend, data layer, networking, security, testing, infrastructure) meant we were looking at a five-digit euro budget and a timeline stretching to today if we'd started back then with the tools available. Fast forward to now, it took me a few weeks and a $20/month Kiro subscription to prototype the same idea. Kiro is officially built by AWS, and while tools like OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor collect most of the attention, Kiro holds its own with comparable capabilities and, in some areas, genuinely better ones. The primary interface is an IDE (VS Code-based), which is how I use it daily, though a CLI option exists for those who prefer terminal workflows similar to Claude Code. There's also Kiro Powers, a kind of extension system developed by open source and third-party partners, and promptz.dev by Christian Bonzelet serves as a cookbook of shared practices and solutions tailored to your specific needs. One tip on getting started: the official docs suggest signing up through kiro.dev, but I find it easier to go through your AWS Account's Amazon Q Developer page instead. From there you can generate sub-accounts, administer them, and use the sign-in URL to authenticate within Kiro. Much cleaner for long-term management, especially if you plan to add team members later. Once you're authenticated, open an empty folder, use the chatbox on the right side, select vibe mode with auto as your model, and ask it to build something small, a single HTML page about your favorite artist, a bash script that sorts files, anything to get a feel for what it can do. From there, you'll naturally progress into more structured workflows like Spec mode, which I'll cover in a future post.

entry.title: Build a webhook-driven email pipeline for your AI agent
entry.summary: Most "AI email" tutorials end with a while True loop that polls an inbox every thirty seconds, runs the new messages through a model, and sends a reply. It demos fine. Then you put it in front of real traffic and the cracks show up immediately: you're burning API calls to fetch nothing 99% of the time, your reaction latency is bounded by your poll interval, and the moment you scale to more than one inbox the polling cost multiplies. Polling an agent's inbox is wasteful. Webhooks are the right primitive for this. The mailbox already knows the instant a message lands — there's no reason to keep asking. entry.title: Make your email agent idempotent against duplicate webhooks
entry.summary: Most posts about "AI email agents" stop at the happy path: webhook fires, model drafts a reply, agent sends it. Demo works, screenshot looks great, ship it. Then it goes to production and the agent replies to the same customer twice ninety seconds apart, and now your "intelligent assistant" looks like a broken cron job. That second reply isn't a bug in your model. It's a property of the delivery system, and it's guaranteed to happen eventually. Nylas webhooks are at-least-once: the same event can arrive up to three times. If your handler treats every POST as a fresh event, every retry is a second action.
